sections.COMMENTS:
The northwestern termination of the Hellenic Arc subduction system in the Ionian Islands area is characterized by a 100 km wide, NE-SW striking, dextral shear zone which accommodates the different styles and velocities of deformation occurring to the north and south. The main structure in this zone is the Kephallonia-Lefkada strike-slip fault that marks the boundary between the oceanic subduction domain to the south and continental collision to the north, this last caused by the presence of the thick continental Apulian block (Shaw and Jackson, 2010). Another NE-SW strike-slip-fault, crossing the Achaia province, seems to mark the southeastern boundary of the shear zone. NW-SE thrust structures also cohexist in the same area, belonging to the accretionary wedge domain of the Hellenic subduction (Kokinou et al., 2005).
The convergence between Africa and the Aegean plates across the Hellenic Arc is thought to take place at ~35 mm/y(Reilinger et al., 2006). GPS velocities of the Aegean plate progressively decrease toward the northwest, where the subduction zone approaches its lateral termination, reaching values of 20-25 mm/y (Hollenstein et al., 2008). North to the Kephallonia-Lefkada fault, convergence between Apulia and the Hellenide domain is in the order of 5-10 mm/y (Hollenstein et al., 2008). The Ionian Island area thus accommodates about 30 mm/y of velocity difference.
Earthquakes show both strike-slip and reverse focal mechanisms (Papazachos et al., 1998; Louvari et al., 1999; Kokinou et al., 2006). P-axis azimuth is around 220Â°N, rotating to 260Â°N while approaching Kephallonia Island (Papazachos et al., 1999).
We propose that this Source is one of the thrust structures belonging to the accretionary wedge of the Hellenic subduction, between the Kephallonia-Lefkada and the Achaia faults. The seismic line ION-7 images it about 50 km to the SW off Zakynthos Island (Kokinou et al., 2005).
The largest recorded seismic event in the area is the Mw 7.2 Kephallonia earthquake of 1953, which caused ca. 0.5 m of vertical displacement (Pirazzoli et al., 1994; Stiros et al., 1994). The focal mechanism reported by McKenzie (1972) for the 1953 event is a thrust and the model by Stiros et al. (1994) based on vertical displacement supports this hypothesis. However, Papazachos et al. (1994) associate this earthquake to the southern portion of the Kephallonia-Lefkada strike-slip fault, on the basis of uplift data and the distribution of seismicity. Another large event took place in 1867, with an estimated magnitude of 7.2, while in 1983 a Mw 7.0 transpressive earthquake occurred on the south-western portion of the Kephallonia-Lefkada fault (Louvari et al., 1999).
Strike, dip and rake of the source are determined taking into consideration the orientation of geologic and bathymetry features together with focal mechanisms data in the area. The depth is inferred on the basis of geological features imaged on the seismic line and of general tectonic considerations.
We also verified that the source kinematics is consistent with the GPS velocity field. Slip rate values are assumed on the basis of general geological and geodynamic considerations.

evidence: Inferred from tectonic and geodynamic considerations.
